headline: Police shot a 1-year-old. Mississippi calls it justified.
summary: Mississippi's attorney general ruled Monday that a Senatobia officer was justified when he fired into a car during a shoplifting call in June, killing 1-year-old Kohen Wiley on his mother's lap. Police say the car drove at officers. His mother says it didn't. No one has been charged, and no video has been released.
cover_answer: Police haven't released it. No one has said why.
table_question: If you say you were right, should you have to show the proof?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: Police in Mississippi thought two women had taken diapers from a store without paying. When their car drove off, an officer fired his gun at it, and a baby still small enough to sit on his mum's lap was hit and died. The grown-ups in charge are still arguing about whether the officer should have fired. You are safe, and the grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: Only if it comes up. A six-year-old can't do anything with this except worry, so the script stays short and ends on safe.
5-7.why_long: A five-year-old takes one vivid feature for the whole event, and here it is a baby on a lap, which is them. Cantor found this age fears what could happen to its own body, so the script keeps the facts small and ends on safe. Expect "could that happen to me?" The true answer: you are here, and the grown-ups have it.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: Senatobia, Mississippi, police got a call about stolen diapers. They say the car drove at them, so an officer fired, and a 1-year-old on his mother's lap died. Monday the state's attorney general ruled it justified. Nobody has seen the video: a referee's call with the replay locked away.
8-12.why: A ruling with the replay locked away. Kids this age want it in the open.
8-12.why_long: This age tests whether adults apply rules fairly, so the script runs the chain: a call about diapers, a car, one shot, a ruling. The referee is the mechanism, and the locked replay lets them judge the process without the facts. Expect "was the officer right?" The state says yes. The family's lawyer says show it.

13-17.script: Mississippi says the officer who shot into a car and killed 1-year-old Kohen Wiley was justified, and nobody has seen the video. Can a ruling be trusted before that? Second: a private autopsy, the family's lawyer says, puts the shot from the side. What does that do to "the car drove at us"?
13-17.why: Two claims and a sealed video. Let them argue from what is missing.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can reason about what is missing, and here that is the video. The script hands them two claims that pull against each other, the ruling and the side-shot autopsy, and asks them to argue from the gap, not fill it. Expect "was it because they're Black?" Protesters say so. The ruling doesn't address it.

5-7.q: Did the baby do something wrong?
5-7.a: No. He was a baby on his mum's lap. The grown-ups are arguing about what the police and the driver did, not about him.

8-12.q: Who decides if the police were right?
8-12.a: The attorney general. She said yes. The family's lawyer says show it.

8-12.q: Why did they shoot at the car?
8-12.a: Police say it drove at an officer. The mum says no. No video yet.

13-17.a: No one has said. The family's lawyer: if it backs the ruling, show it.

13-17.q: Can police shoot at a moving car?
13-17.a: An expert told AP: get out of the way. His lawyer: he had no choice.
